one_liner: Pure-Java multithreaded FFT/DCT/DST/DHT library; beat a per-call-planned FFTW (via JNI) on smooth 2-D/3-D sizes, lost on primes.
what_it_does: Provides 1-D, 2-D and 3-D DFT, DCT, DST and DHT in double and float precision (DoubleFFT_1D, FloatFFT_2D, DoubleDCT_3D, ...) for the JVM, with no native code. You construct a plan object for a size, then call in-place methods such as complexForward(a), complexInverse(a, scale), realForward(a) or realForwardFull(a) on interleaved double[]/float[] arrays, or on JLargeArrays objects for arrays beyond 2^31 elements. The API is its own, not FFTW-compatible.
how_it_is_fast: The constructor picks one of three algorithms: Ooura's split-radix FFT for powers of two, FFTPack-derived mixed-radix (factors 4, 2, 3, 5, plus generic odd factors) when what remains after those factors is below 211, and Bluestein's chirp-z algorithm (zero-padded to the next power of two at or above 2n-1) otherwise. Twiddle and bit-reversal tables are precomputed in the constructor. Above size thresholds (1-D: 8,192 elements for 2 threads, 65,536 for 4; 2-D/3-D: 65,536) the butterflies and row/column passes are split across a JLargeArrays ConcurrencyUtils thread pool. There is no explicit SIMD.
when_to_use: JVM applications (Java, Kotlin, Scala) that need FFT, DCT, DST or DHT without JNI or native libraries, e.g. image processing (the companion paper is on large-scale image deblurring).

Large 2-D or 3-D real/complex transforms on multi-core machines, where the built-in threading helps: in FFTBench, threaded JTransforms ran 1,920x1,080 in 0.125 s vs 0.360 s for single-threaded FFTW via ezFFTW.
Power-of-two or 2/3/5-smooth sizes (image dimensions like 1280x720, 3000x2000), which use the split-radix or mixed-radix paths.
1-D arrays larger than 2^31 elements, through DoubleLargeArray/FloatLargeArray (changelog 3.0: sizes up to 2^63).
when_not_to_use: C or C++ code: this is Java only; native projects should use FFTW, PocketFFT or a sibling C/C++ library.

Sizes with large prime factors: they go to Bluestein; in FFTBench the prime 1-D size 589,829 (1.052 vs 0.815 s) and the prime-by-prime 1,087x1,931 2-D case (single-threaded 2.132 vs 0.998 s) lost to even a per-call FFTW_ESTIMATE baseline.
Non-power-of-two DoubleFFT_1D.realInverse: open issue #21 (2020) reports output with twice the expected amplitude (example size 48).
Workloads where you could use properly planned native FFTW: the only FFTW comparison found re-plans FFTW_ESTIMATE on every call through JNI, so JTransforms has not been shown to beat tuned FFTW.
Allocation- or latency-sensitive loops: the mixed-radix and Bluestein paths allocate scratch arrays on every call (new double[...] in the source), adding GC pressure.

integration.dependencies: JLargeArrays (org.visnow; 1.7 for release 3.2 per the changelog, 1.8-SNAPSHOT in the HEAD pom); Apache Commons Math was dropped in 3.2
integration.min_toolchain: HEAD pom compiles with --release 11 and adds module-info.java; JTransforms 3.1 ran on Java 8 (JDK 1.8.0_111) in FFTBench
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Thread count and the size thresholds for threading are process-wide static settings (CommonUtils, JLargeArrays ConcurrencyUtils), and the internal pool uses non-daemon threads.

gotchas: The internal thread pool uses non-daemon threads, so main() can hang about 60 s before the JVM exits (open issue #14); call ConcurrencyUtils.shutdownThreadPoolAndAwaitTermination() or set the thread count to 1.
realForward returns a packed half spectrum in place (for even n, a[1] holds Re[n/2]); realForwardFull needs an array of length 2n with only the first n filled, and its inverse is complexInverse.
Inverse transforms take a boolean scale flag; pass true to get 1/n normalisation.
Open issue #15 (2018): FloatFFT_2D.realForwardFull hangs at 4,098x4,097 right after a 4,096x4,096 call succeeds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling is a Java library; pick JTransforms when you must stay on the JVM without native code. For C/C++ code, PocketFFT or KFR cover the same transforms faster, and FFTW itself remains the reference.
verified_claims_summary: Third-party FFTBench (JMH 1.21, Oracle JDK 1.8.0_111, AMD Phenom II X4 955, Ubuntu 16.04, 2-3 iterations) ran a real-to-complex forward, DC-zero and inverse round trip with JTransforms 3.1 against FFTW through the ezFFTW 0.1.2 JNI wrapper, which plans FFTW_ESTIMATE inside every call. Single-threaded JTransforms won on smooth 2-D sizes (1.13x at 1280x720 up to 1.40x at 5000x5000) and on 256^3 (1.87x), but lost at 1,087x1,931, 100x120x140 and 400x300x200; threaded 1-D JTransforms won at 10,000,000 elements (1.42x) but lost at 98,304, 589,829 and 1,000,000 (ratios derived from page data).
status_note: Active again after ten quiet years (3.1 in 2015, 3.2 released November 2025, last commit 2025-12-05); BSD-2-Clause and on Maven Central, though several correctness and hang issues (#15, #21) are still open.
